resources.string: Picture chain checks, test patterns and a calibration guide for your TV
What the box knows about the TV: resolution, refresh rates, HDR and Dolby Vision
Step by step through the TV settings, for SDR, HDR10 and Dolby Vision
What each source returned. Some are blocked for apps on this box; the checks combine the ones that work.
HDR formats turned off on the box
The box sends 4K. Test patterns can be shown pixel for pixel.
The box is not sending 4K. On the box: Settings › Display & Sound › Advanced display settings › Resolution › 2160p.
The current mode could not be read.
24, 25, 50 and 60 Hz are all available in 4K, so films and TV can play at their own rate.
No 24 Hz mode in 4K: films will judder. Something in the chain (Sync Box, soundbar, cable) is limiting the modes.
25 or 50 Hz is missing in 4K: European and Israeli broadcasts will judder.
The box shows apps only its current mode. The practical 24 Hz test (stage 2) checks frame rate switching for real.
The TV accepts HDR10 through the chain.
HDR10 is not reported. Check that HDMI 2 is set to the enhanced / HDMI 2.1 format on the TV and that the Sync Box and soundbar pass HDR.
The TV accepts Dolby Vision through the chain.
The HDMI driver sees Dolby Vision from the TV. Android hides it from apps on this box, which is harmless: players use the driver.

Dolby Vision is not reported. The Hue Sync Box, the soundbar or the cable is probably blocking it: in the Hue app turn on Dolby Vision for this input, check the soundbar\'s 4K/HDR passthrough, use an Ultra High Speed cable.
Formats that are nice to have; calibration uses HDR10 and Dolby Vision.
The TV declares its peak, average and minimum brightness.
The EDID declares no brightness values. The TV does its own tone mapping so this is usually harmless; the soundbar or Sync Box may be replacing the TV\'s EDID.

These look like Android\'s defaults (peak = average, minimum 0), not values from the TV. The raw EDID is not readable by apps on this box; earlier adb showed it declares none. Harmless: the TV does its own tone mapping.
The declared brightness could not be read.
On: the box switches to the content\'s frame rate (for example 24 Hz for films).

Set to \"seamless only\". Over HDMI switching is never seamless, so in practice it never switches. On the box: Settings › Display & Sound › Advanced display settings › Match content frame rate › Always.
Off: films play at 60 Hz and judder. On the box: Settings › Display & Sound › Advanced display settings › Match content frame rate › Always.
This setting could not be read. You will be asked about it in the summary (stage 2).
Passthrough: HDR content reaches the TV as it is.
The system may convert HDR formats. For calibration choose passthrough (on the box: Settings › Display & Sound › Advanced display settings › HDR format preference).
The box forces one HDR output format, so the TV never sees the content\'s own format. Switch to passthrough.
This box does not report HDR conversion.
No HDR format is turned off.
These formats are turned off on the box: content in them reaches the TV converted or as SDR. Turn them back on in the box\'s display settings.
The colour format the box sends right now. For HDR it should switch to 10 or 12 bit; the HDR test in stage 2 checks this while HDR plays.
The HDMI output format is not readable by apps on this box.
Hardware decoders for 4K HEVC 10-bit and Dolby Vision are present.
No Dolby Vision decoder is reported to apps. Dolby Vision may play only as HDR10.
No 4K60 HEVC 10-bit decoder: the 4K test patterns cannot play.
The decoder list could not be read.
4K video patterns, played on the box\'s video plane: pixel for pixel, no upscaling.
Hardware decoder (%1$s) reproduces all %2$d patterns bit for bit.
Hardware decoder (%1$s) reproduces all %2$d patterns (checked in 8 bits: the decoder hands apps only an 8-bit copy).
Decoder check not possible on this box: %1$s

Set Brightness. Raise it until bar 12 (below black) shows, then lower it until 12 just disappears while 20 is still faintly visible. Correct: 12 invisible, 20 and 25 visible, and the steps from about 18 up can be told apart. 20 invisible means shadows are crushed (too low); 12 visible means black is grey (too high).

Set Contrast. Correct: every patch up to 235 is distinct from its neighbours and the white stays neutral (no yellow, pink or blue tint). If 230–235 merge, Contrast is too high; lower it until they separate. Patches above 235 may merge: that is allowed.

Check gamma and banding. Correct: the 11 steps rise evenly and all look neutral grey; the ramps are smooth, and the dark 0–20 % ramp shows no blotches or coloured bands. In SDR the box sends 8 bits, so the 10-bit and 8-bit ramps look alike: that is expected. Strong steps in both mean processing (noise reduction, dynamic contrast).

Check colour. Correct: clean bars with sharp borders and no glow; 75 % white looks neutral (a little warm in the Warm setting). Glowing, cartoon-like colours mean a vivid/colour enhancer is on or the colour space is not Auto.

Set Sharpness. Lower it until no bright or dark halos run along the thin lines on grey. Native 4K is proven when the 1 px lines are distinct from 20–30 cm. The 1 px checkerboard is the finest detail possible: if it is flat grey even up close, something in the chain filters it (see the Resolution pattern). Moiré or shimmering means super resolution or sharpening is on.

Look from 20–30 cm. Correct: every square shows its pattern. On this setup the 1 px checkerboards stay grey: the box\'s noise reduction (Amlogic, not switchable without root) removes that one finest detail, while 1 px lines, diagonals and 2 px detail get through. The TV\'s own player shows them, so the panel is fine. Real content is barely affected.

Check the picture size. Correct: all four outer white edges are visible and the grey frames every 2 px are sharp and separate. A missing edge means the TV crops the picture: turn on Just scan / Screen fit / Overscan off.

In HDR picture mode, set Brightness (or Black level / Shadow detail). Correct: bar 56 (below black) is invisible, 72 and 80 are faintly visible, and the steps from about 68 up can be told apart. Local dimming may swallow the darkest small steps: judge with the dimming setting you will watch with.

The TV receives metadata for a 1000-nit master. Correct: every patch up to 1000 is distinct (the TV reaches it or rolls off gently); above that they may merge. If 700–1000 already merge, brightness is being limited (Eco, light sensor, dynamic tone mapping set too strong).

The same with metadata for a 4000-nit master: the TV should compress 4000 nits into its own range, so 1500–4000 should still be distinguishable, with less contrast. If everything above about 1000 is one white, the TV clips instead of mapping.
Steps in absolute nits. Correct: an even, clean rise with neutral greys; the ramps are smooth without bands (this is where 10 bits matter); the 0–10 nit ramp shows the shadow detail.

A 1000-nit box glides over black. Correct: little halo around it, the black around it stays black, and zones do not jump as it crosses them. A large halo, or a box that dims while moving: adjust Local dimming (usually High or Medium).

White subtitles on black, the hardest case for local dimming. Correct: the black around the letters is almost the same as the rest of the screen. A light-grey band around the lines is blooming: lower Local dimming one step, or keep it if overall black matters more to you.

Small stars on black. Correct: the stars are clearly visible, even the smallest, and the background is black. Stars that vanish or dim mean the dimming is too aggressive; a grey haze around them is blooming.

A pan at 23.976 fps; the display switches to 24 Hz for it. Film-like and correct: motion with slight, even steps (the natural judder of 24p) and no soap-opera look. Perfectly smooth motion means MEMC is on; uneven steps (long-short) mean the display stayed at 60 Hz (3:2 pulldown).
Plays clips at 23.976, 25 and 50 fps and checks that the display really switches to their rate. The screen blanks for a moment at each switch: that is normal. About half a minute.
The test needs the test files: open Test patterns first so they download.
%1$s fps · explicit request (like a dedicated player)
%1$s fps · ExoPlayer\'s default request (like most streaming apps)
The screen blanks for a moment at every HDMI mode change: expected.
The display switched to exactly the content\'s rate: even motion, no pulldown.
The display switched to 24.000 Hz instead of 23.976: one frame repeats about every 42 s. Rarely noticeable.
The display switched to a multiple of the rate (for example 50 Hz for 25 fps): every frame shows twice, evenly. Fine.
The display did not switch. Check that the box\'s Match content frame rate is Always and that the Sync Box and soundbar pass the mode.
The display switched to a rate that does not fit the content.
With the default request (only if seamless) the display did not switch: over HDMI no switch is seamless. Apps that ask this way play at 60 Hz; that is the app, not your settings.
Even with the default request the display switched: the system switches for every app.
